steps.caption: A beginner sees the rook aimed at the king and thinks White is lost. Look closer: White can take that rook for free. Missing an answer like this loses games that were not lost. This lesson teaches you to find every answer.
The black rook on e8 looks straight down the e-file (the column of squares marked e) at the white king. Nothing stands between them, so White is in **check**.

steps.text: A king is in **check** when an enemy piece attacks it. You must answer at once, and there are exactly three ways: **move** the king to a safe square, **block** by putting a piece between the checker and the king, or **capture** the checking piece. Next, each way is shown on this same board, one at a time.

steps.caption: Way one, move the king. A check is over when the king stands on a square no enemy piece attacks.

line.say: The king steps sideways off the e-file, out of the rook's line.

steps.caption: Way two, block. Put your own piece on a square between the checker and the king.

line.say: The bishop slides between the two. The rook now attacks the bishop, not the king.

steps.caption: Way three, capture. A piece that has been taken cannot give check.

line.say: The white rook takes the checking rook along the eighth rank. Nothing attacks the king now.

steps.text: You may never ignore a check, and you may never make a move that leaves your own king attacked. That is why, in the board below, the game allows only seven moves out of all those White has.

steps.caption: The seven allowed moves: four king steps, two blocks, one capture. Every other white move leaves the king attacked.
Legal is not the same as good. Block on e6 and the bishop is unguarded: the rook just takes it.

line.say: The bishop blocks, but nothing guards it.
The rook takes it for free, and the white king is exposed again.

steps.caption: Block on e2 instead and the king guards the bishop. If the rook takes it, the king takes the rook back.

line.say: The bishop blocks and the king guards it.
Taking would trade a rook for a bishop.
The king recaptures, and Black has lost the exchange.

steps.text: Compare what is left afterwards. A **free capture** removes the checker and costs nothing. A **guarded block** holds. An **unguarded block** gives the piece away. [I] As a default tendency, look for the free capture first, then a guarded block, then a king step, and use an unguarded block last. This is a habit, not a law: sometimes the position says otherwise.

steps.caption: A bishop checks along a diagonal, so every way out exists. The pawn on a3 can capture it, the pawn or the knight can block on c3, the knight can block on d2, or the king can step.
The queen checks from the square next to the king. The bishop on g5 guards that square, so the king may not take the queen.

line.say: The only legal move: the king steps away. A king may never go to an attacked square.

steps.caption: Same check, but now nothing guards the queen. This time the king can capture it.

line.say: The king takes the queen. It is safe on d2 because no black piece attacks that square.

steps.title: Guarded or not?
steps.prompt: Same queen, same square, same check. One feature differs between the positions. Predict first for each, then check.

steps.caption: White is in check from the rook, and the knight looks able to block on e2. But the bishop on b4 pins the knight to the king: if the knight moved, the bishop would attack the king. So the block is illegal.
steps.chapter: A way out must be safe

steps.text: A **pinned** piece cannot move off the line between an enemy piece and its own king. So a pinned blocker or capturer does not count as a way out. A way out counts only if the move leaves your own king safe. Add that to your three tests.

steps.title: Pinned or free?
steps.prompt: Same rook check, same knight. One feature differs between the positions. Predict first for each, then check.

steps.caption: A knight gives check from f3. It jumps, so no piece can stand between it and the king. Only two kinds of answer exist: take the knight, or move the king.

line.say: The queen captures the knight. Nothing else could stop this check except a king move.

steps.text: A check can be blocked only if there is at least one empty square between the checker and the king. Rooks, bishops and queens checking from a distance leave such a gap. A **knight**, a **pawn**, or any piece checking from the next square leaves none, so you may only capture the checker or move the king. A pawn attacks the two squares diagonally in front of it.

steps.caption: A pawn checks too, from the square diagonally in front of it. There is no gap to block, so the king takes it.

line.say: The king captures the pawn. Nothing guards it, so the king is safe.

steps.text: Sometimes all three ways fail. Then it is **checkmate**: the game ends and the player in check loses. Emanuel Lasker, in his lectures, counted mate as control of up to nine squares: the king's own and its neighbours. He added that the checking piece must be safe. Both parts are the three tests [S]. So before you say mate, test each way in turn: step, block, capture.

steps.caption: Here White can win at once. Look at the black king and its own pawns.

line.say: The rook takes the rook and gives check along the back rank (the edge row where that player's pieces start).

steps.caption: Test one, the king. Its three pawns fill the squares in front. The rook covers f8, and its line runs through the king, so h8 is no escape either.
Tests two and three. No black piece can reach e8 or f8 to block, and none can capture the rook. All three ways fail, so this is checkmate.
Now Black has one more piece, a knight on d7. The rook checks, the king has no square, but the knight can block.

line.say: The knight jumps to f8, between the rook and the king. The check is answered, so this was not mate.

steps.caption: Another version: Black has a rook on a8. The king still has no square, but the rook sees the checker.

line.say: The black rook captures the checking rook. The check is gone, so this was not mate.

steps.caption: A queen can mate near the edge when the king guards her. White to move.

line.say: The queen lands on g7, guarded by the white king. The black king cannot take her and every other square is covered.

steps.caption: Now the white king stands on g5 and does not guard g7. Same queen move. White gave the queen away: after the king takes her, only bare kings remain, a draw.

line.say: The same queen move gives check.
But nothing guards her, so the king captures her. Check, not mate.

steps.title: One pawn, opposite results
steps.prompt: Same rook check on the back rank. Which position is checkmate? Predict first, then check. Choose check, checkmate or neither.

steps.caption: A double check: two pieces check at once. Taking the knight does not help because the rook still checks. Only a king move helps.
steps.chapter: When only one way is left

line.say: The king steps aside. One block or one capture could never answer both checks at once.

steps.text: Three habits. Habit one: list all three ways before you move; do not assume the king can step away. Habit two: after your own move, check which opposing checks you leave open. Dan Heisman recommends listing the opponent's checks, captures and threats before you move [S, chess.com article]. [H] Beginners may forget the capture most, because taking feels like attacking, not defending; this is a guess, not data.

steps.caption: Not every long line is check. The rook points at the king, but White's pawn stands in the way, so there is nothing to answer.

steps.prompt: Explain to a friend, using the first board of this lesson, why White is not checkmated. Say it aloud or write it down, then compare with the model explanation next.

steps.text: **A model explanation.** White is in check from the rook on e8, but it is not mate. Test one, the king: it can step to d1, d2, f1 or f2. Test two, block: the bishop can go to e2 or e6. Test three, capture: the rook on a8 takes the rook on e8. One working way is enough, so the game goes on. The best one wins a whole rook.

steps.prompt: Think of the last position you hesitated on. Which of the three ways did you forget to look at first: the king's squares, a block, or a capture?
